questions.question: In the CAP theorem, what does 'Consistency' mean?
options: The system never crashes
Every read receives the most recent write or an error
Data is stored on at least two nodes
The system responds within a fixed time limit
questions.explanation: CAP consistency means linearizability: every read returns the most recently completed write. All nodes appear to have the same data at the same time.

questions.question: In the CAP theorem, 'Availability' means:
options: The system has 99.99% uptime
Every request receives a non-error response, without guarantee it contains the most recent write
At least one node is always running
The system can handle unlimited traffic
questions.explanation: CAP availability means every request to a non-failing node gets a response. The response might not reflect the latest write, but the system doesn't refuse to answer.

questions.question: A network partition in the context of CAP refers to:
options: Splitting the database into shards
A break in network communication between nodes, preventing them from syncing
Dividing users into groups
A planned maintenance window
questions.explanation: A network partition is a communication failure between nodes. Some nodes cannot reach others, even though each node individually is still running. The CAP theorem addresses what happens during this scenario.

questions.question: During a network partition, a CP system will:
options: Continue serving all requests with possibly stale data
Refuse to serve requests that can't be guaranteed consistent
Automatically repair the network
Delete all data on the partitioned node
questions.explanation: A CP system prioritizes consistency. During a partition, it will block or reject requests rather than risk returning stale or inconsistent data. Availability is sacrificed.

questions.question: Which of the following is an AP (Available + Partition-tolerant) system?
options: Google Spanner
etcd
DynamoDB
ZooKeeper
questions.explanation: DynamoDB is designed for high availability. During partitions, it continues accepting reads and writes, resolving conflicts later through mechanisms like last-writer-wins or vector clocks.

questions.question: The CAP theorem states that during a network partition, a distributed system can guarantee at most:
options: All three: consistency, availability, and partition tolerance
Either consistency or availability, but not both
Only partition tolerance
None of the three properties
questions.explanation: CAP proves that when a partition occurs, a system must choose between consistency (all nodes agree) and availability (all nodes respond). You cannot have both simultaneously during a partition.

questions.question: PACELC extends the CAP theorem by adding:
options: A fourth property: Durability
The trade-off between Latency and Consistency when there is no partition
Support for multi-region deployments
Automatic partition detection
questions.explanation: PACELC says: if Partition → choose A or C; Else → choose L (latency) or C (consistency). It captures the everyday trade-off: even without partitions, strong consistency adds latency.

questions.question: Eventual consistency means:
options: Data is always consistent across all nodes
If no new writes occur, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value
Consistency is never achieved
Only the leader node has correct data
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency guarantees that, given enough time without new writes, all replicas will converge to the same value. There's a window where reads may return stale data, but the system eventually catches up.

questions.question: Google Spanner achieves strong consistency across global data centers primarily by using:
options: Eventual consistency with conflict resolution
Synchronized atomic clocks (TrueTime) to order transactions globally
A single leader in one data center
Client-side caching
questions.explanation: Spanner uses TrueTime, a globally synchronized clock system based on GPS and atomic clocks, to assign globally meaningful timestamps to transactions, enabling strong consistency across continents.

questions.question: A common misconception about CAP is that you 'pick two out of three.' Why is this misleading?
options: Because you can actually have all three
Because partition tolerance is not optional in distributed systems — the real choice is between C and A during a partition
Because CAP only applies to single-node systems
Because the theorem has been disproven
questions.explanation: Network partitions will happen in any distributed system, so partition tolerance is mandatory, not optional. The real choice is what your system does DURING a partition: maintain consistency (CP) or availability (AP).
